title: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Compression ↔ Intimacy's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal. One synthetic voice, whisper to shout, runs all three pieces on one engine: for the technical side, the voice carried away in open air to show that distance adds no range, then the page's own whisper-and-shout pair built with the range in the act, where a pair made equal fails; for the vulnerability parallel, the four knobs turned against the page's line for each, to the release line where they part; for the teaching, the page's Part 1 matched in loudness, with a close microphone's bass as the control, walked up to 24 blind pairs asking where the singer is. Advanced Applications has no piece: a parallel-compression blend on this voice would only confirm what the page already says it does, and its felt claim needs the same ear the blind test asks for. The Vulnerability Parallel is a ### heading, so its piece sits in The Conceptual Side and is approved with it. I grow when a listener's scores come back, or when a real vocal take can stand beside the synthetic one. I never hold the entry's words.

verdicts.file: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich — does distance narrow a voice.html
verdicts.why: Its test can't fail (open-air distance is one gain, so range is fixed by arithmetic), and it builds the page's pair with whisper and shout given the same 4 dB range, then reports they don't differ in range; made wider (12 dB), the shout arrives at 50 m with 7.21 dB against the whisper's 4.00 at 5 cm, the page's way. Remake: say the null is arithmetic, let the reader set the pair's made ranges, measure across consonants or say it doesn't, drop 'What is enormous in the pair is not range'.

pieces.file: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich — does distance narrow a voice.html
pieces.title: Does distance narrow a voice? · a whisper in your ear, a shout across a field
pieces.caption: **Does distance make a voice’s range, or does the act?** One synthetic phrase, a pulse and noise through formant filters, nobody recorded: whisper to shout, 32 dB from its quietest syllable to its loudest at 5 cm. Three steps. The phrase at the microphone. The singer carried away in open air to 50 m: in this model distance is one gain on the whole voice, so the range can’t move, and the piece says that is arithmetic; only a quiet floor changes it, and only by narrowing (27.9 dB at 4 m, 12.2 at 32 m). Last, the page’s own pair with the range in the act, where the sentence puts it: a whisper made with 4 dB in your ear, a shout made with 4, 12 or 20 dB at 50 or 100 m. The rule is set before you choose: the pair holds when the shout reaches you wider than the whisper. The control, made equal, fails (3.17 dB at 50 m); a 12 dB shout holds at 50 m (7.21) and fails at 100 m (3.73), the floor taking it. The range you hear is the range the act made, less what the floor takes. Range is measured over vowels; consonants are left out. The effort-against-level cue (Brungart and Scott, JASA 2001) is carried with its caveat: it holds for voiced speech, and for whispers judged distance didn’t follow effort. Rooms were tried and left out: across twelve, the range at 8 m moved −2.5 to +3.6 dB, by each room’s colour.
pieces.near: Our ears interpret small dynamic range as proximity

verdicts.why: Walks up and finds a real seam in the page's four-knob map, but step 5 says 'The test can fail: if a slower release held them down less', which a one-pole release cannot do. Replace that one sentence with: the meter can't go the other way; what is under test is which way the page reads the hold. Nothing else changes.

pieces.file: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich — four knobs and the guard.html
pieces.title: Four knobs and the guard · the vulnerability parallel, measured
pieces.caption: **Which way does the hold point?** The 4:1 voice from the blind test below, with its gain reduction drawn under it, then each knob turned against the page’s line for it. Threshold: below it nothing is held; at −30 dB it touches 4 of 7 syllables, at −10 none. Ratio: 1:1 holds nothing; ∞:1 pins the shout to the threshold, −30.1 dB. Attack: at 50 ms the shout’s start stands 8.2 dB above its held part, at 1 ms 2.3. Those three lines read the hold as the guard. Last, release. The meter can’t go the other way, a slower release always holds longer, so what is tested is the page’s reading of the hold: on the guard reading a slow release keeps the guard up, and the page says it keeps you open. Measured: at 1 s the soft line after the shout is held 11.0 dB where its own level asks 1.8, the whisper after it 7.0, and the extra hold lasts 1.38 s; at 40 ms, 1.9 dB, 0.0 and 79 ms. The release line holds only if the hold is the closeness, which is how the page’s opening and its Part 3 read compression. The Vulnerability Parallel is a ### heading, so this piece sits in, and is approved with, The Conceptual Side.

verdicts.file: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich — where is the singer.html
verdicts.why: A real blind test of Part 1: chance (9/256 per edge) and rule stated first, all three sets scored, loudness confirmed at −20.0 LUFS by ffmpeg ebur128 on the rendered buffers, no leak by length, start, onset, wobble or pumping. Note: 'level, not colour' holds inside vowels only (consonants rise +4.7 and +7.0 dB at 4:1), and the brightness leak is unclosed, not unclosable.

pieces.file: Compression ↔ Intimacy — rich — where is the singer.html
pieces.title: Where is the singer? · Part 1, blind, with a control
pieces.caption: **Where is the singer, when only the range changes?** Part 1 on a synthetic voice: uncompressed, 4:1 (threshold −30 dB, 10 and 120 ms) and 20:1 (−44 dB, 1 and 40 ms), each matched to −20 LUFS by BS.1770-4 gated loudness measured in the piece; and a fourth, the uncompressed voice through a cardioid’s proximity effect at 5 cm (+7.7 dB at 200 Hz against 1 kHz), the control that tells range from spectral tilt. Four steps walk up to 24 blind pairs, eight for each version against the uncompressed one, order and side random, asking which singer is closer. The rule is set before the first pair: 7 or 8 of 8 reads closer (1 in 28 by guessing), 0 or 1 farther, and the page’s claim is read from the 4:1 set alone. Leaks checked and printed: equal length and start; inside each vowel the compressor changes level, not colour (0.14 dB at most; the consonants before the half voice and the shout rise 4.7 and 7.0 dB against their vowels at 4:1, the range narrowing inside the syllable), while the shelf lifts below 300 Hz by 4.7 to 8.1 dB; the 20:1 gain moves 0.62 dB inside the held shout (residue −47 dB) and, looking 5 ms ahead, adds no click at the onsets. Three aren’t closed here, and the piece says so: no match holds every reading of level (the uncompressed voice’s loudest 400 ms are 2.9 dB above the 20:1’s, its average 2.9 dB below); raising the breathy whispers brightens the phrase (+7.2 dB above 3 kHz at 4:1), unclosed rather than unclosable, since a version brightened to match would close it; and a listener who can hear which one is compressed can answer the page instead of the singer. Whether 20:1 sounds fake is not scored. No listener has taken it yet.

offers.what: Reduced after the challenge (the maker’s claim-change was disputed: the sentence predicates range of the act, not of distance, and the face’s own engine bears that reading out once a shout is made wider). The sentence could say where the range lives: “a whispered voice in your ear is made with little range; a shout across a field is made with a lot.” Measured on “does distance narrow a voice”: distance adds no range (in open air it is one gain; a quiet floor only narrows it), so what reaches you is the range the act made, less what the floor takes: a shout made 12 dB wide arrives with 7.21 dB at 50 m against the whisper’s 4.00 at 5 cm, and with 3.73 at 100 m. If Loudon wants more, an addition, not a correction, for voiced speech only: listeners judge voiced speech farther the harder it was made and nearer the louder it arrives (Brungart & Scott 2001, JASA 110(1):425–440, doi 10.1121/1.1379730, abstract read); the same abstract says whispered speech’s judged distance was unaffected by production level, so it says nothing for the whisper. Whether a narrower range sounds closer stays open on a listener’s score in the blind test under Teaching the Resonance.

Confirmed by the challenger as a reading. The Vulnerability Parallel presents its four lines as one map (“Compression parameters map to intimacy”), but its release line runs against the other three, and the page never names it. Threshold, ratio and attack read gain reduction as the guard: no hold is “safe to be authentic”, ∞:1 is “complete guard up”, a fast attack is “immediate defense”. On that reading a slow release keeps the guard up after the moment passes. On “four knobs and the guard”: at 1 s the soft line after the shout is held 10.99 dB where its own level asks 1.82, the whisper after it 6.97 dB, the extra hold lasting 1.38 s; at 40 ms, 1.93 dB, 0.00 dB and 79 ms. The meter can’t go the other way, so the numbers show the reading, they don’t prove it. The page says “Slow release: Stay open longer”, true only if the hold is the closeness, as the page’s opening, the section’s own first subsection (“Loud ↓ … Defenses ↓ … → Intimacy”) and Part 3 read it. Two ways home, Loudon’s choice: turn the release line (“Release = how long the guard stays up after the moment passes. Fast release: back to open quickly. Slow release: guarded long after.”), or name the double reading as a contradiction the page holds: the compressor is both the guard and the closeness.

Confirmed in part by the challenger. The table mixes the same two readings as the Conceptual Side offer: “Fast attack = guarded | Quick defense = guarded” reads the hold as the guard; “Reduces loud peaks | Reduces defensive reactions” and “Slow release = sustain | Sustained openness = deep connection” read it as the closeness. “Controlled by threshold | Controlled by trust” is neutral and doesn’t count. Carry with the Conceptual Side offer; whichever way that goes, this table follows. A separate slip, a no-claim-edit candidate: “Creates proximity effect” names a close microphone’s bass rise, not something a compressor does; this face’s own control shows the two apart (+7.7 dB at 200 Hz from a cardioid at 5 cm, range unchanged). E.g. “Creates a sense of proximity”.
